papers.paper: Lanke (1974), Interval Estimation of a Median, Scand. J. Statist. 1:28-32
papers.pages_read: All 6 (p.1 JSTOR cover; pp.2-6 content): text layer for all; p.3 (Theorem 2 statement and proof) additionally checked as a rendered image because the exponent in the text layer was garbled.
papers.what_it_proves: Setting: i.i.d. sample X1..Xn from a continuous distribution, symmetric about an unknown centre theta (median/mode); infinite population, sampling with replacement. Thm 1: for continuous symmetric unimodal F, P(X(1)-lam*R < theta < X(n)+lam*R) >= 1-(2+2lam)^{-(n-1)}, R = range; sharp (uniform). A=0 gives the variation interval with coverage 1-2^{-(n-1)}. Thm 2 (impossibility): for no alpha < 2^{-n+1} do there exist real, locally bounded measurable functions g_L, g_R on R^n with P(g_L(X)<theta<g_R(X)) >= 1-alpha for ALL continuous distributions symmetric about theta. Thm 3: the coverage lower bound for quasi-range intervals is attained at the rectangular distribution. Thm 4: for merely unimodal (non-symmetric) F, coverage >= 1-(1+lam)^{-(n-1)}, sharp.
papers.detail: WHAT IS CLAIMED. Theorem 2 as printed reads 'For no alpha < 2^{-n+1}', i.e. n < 1 + log2(1/alpha). The matching possibility is the variation interval, with miscoverage exactly 2^{-(n-1)} (Thm 1 at lam=0; the text just before Thm 1 calls 1-2^{-n+1} the largest coverage obtainable by order-statistic interpolation methods). So the threshold in the statement is sharp: log2(1/alpha) + 1 vs n. It is NOT log2(2/alpha) vs n in a different form: 1+log2(1/alpha)=log2(2/alpha). CAVEAT ON THE PROOF AS PRINTED: the proof says 'obviously sufficient' to show that no locally bounded g_R satisfies P(g_R(X)<=theta) <= gamma for any gamma < 2^{-n}, and then derives gamma >= P(X in K)=2^{-n}. It never displays the step from one-sided gamma<2^{-n} to two-sided alpha<2^{-n+1}. A literal reading of the printed argument gives only alpha<2^{-n} (n < log2(1/alpha)), a one-bit gap to the stated theorem; I could not reconstruct the factor 2 from the printed text (the construction uses one cluster pair per theta, so the left-end failure is not forced simultaneously). Treat the sharp 1+log2(1/alpha) as 'stated by Lanke, proof only sketched at the factor 2'. A closing remark says the median can be made unique with gamma >= (2+eps)^{-n}, again one-sided. PROCEDURE CLASS: all measurable, locally bounded endpoint pairs (g_L,g_R) on R^n. No equivariance assumed (a strictly larger class than location-scale equivariant), but 'locally bounded' is an explicit restriction (endpoints must be finite reals; infinite intervals are excluded, unlike (A) where unbounded intervals are allowed and counted). The proof is a pure translation argument: X i.i.d. uniform on [-1,1] union [2*theta-1, 2*theta+1], theta chosen above sup of g_R on the cube [-1,1]^n, so all-n-in-left-cluster (prob 2^{-n}) forces g_R<=theta. No scale argument is used. POPULATIONS: continuous distributions only (no atoms), symmetric about theta; the extremal population is a two-cluster uniform mixture (two far-apart intervals), not a two-point population. Atoms are not treated, but impossibility over a subclass transfers to any superclass containing it, so atoms do not hurt the impossibility direction. RELATION TO (A): contains the large-G, smallest-kappa0 NUMBER n<1+log2(1/alpha) (modulo the factor-2 caveat) for an infinite-population, with-replacement, symmetric-centre problem with arbitrary finite-valued procedures. Does NOT contain: finite population, simple random sampling without replacement, fpc-t interval, max-share kappa, pi(k) or k*, kappa2(k*-1), the 'unbounded with probability >= pi(k*-1)-alpha under every population' statement, the fixed-coefficient residual setting, or minimaxity of SRS among fixed-size designs. Its extremal object is a two-cluster population (an outlier-dominated sample with all n draws in one cluster), conceptually the coarse limit of (A)'s 'all sampled clusters in the constant block', but there is no quantitative interpolation in G, k, or kappa. Nothing on (B).

papers.paper: Bakirov & Szekely (2006), Student's t-test for Gaussian scale mixtures, J. Math. Sci. 139(3):6497-6505
papers.pages_read: All 9 (text layer, read in full including proofs, appendix, tables and references). The page images queued by read_file were not delivered to me; formulas in the text layer are partly garbled but legible, and no image cross-check was done.
papers.what_it_proves: Setting: X_1..X_n independent N(mu, sigma_k^2) with unequal variances (equivalent by integration to i.i.d. Gaussian scale mixtures; Thm 2). s_{n-1}(x) = sup over sigma_k >= 0 of P(|T_n|>x), with T_n the usual t-statistic. Thm 1: for n>=2, x>=0, the sup equals max over R<k<=n of the t_{k-1} tail at sqrt(R(k-1)/(k-R)), R = n x^2/(x^2+n-1); equals 1 (two-sided) / 1/2 (one-sided) for x<1, 3/4 one-sided at x=1, and equals the ordinary t_{n-1} tail for x >= sqrt(3(n-1)/(n-3)). Proof: reduce to a quadratic form, eigenvalue lemma, integral representation, then a second-derivative argument showing that at a maximum all nonzero x_k = R*sigma_k^2 are equal. Proposition: unique crossing points r(k) of the t_k and t_{k+1} tails with r(k) -> 3. Corollary 2: Phi*(x)=lim s_n(x). Tables of one-sided critical values. For symmetric unimodal (Khintchine mixtures of uniforms) they only state, without proof, that the analogous function u_{n-1}(x) (sup over k of sums of uniforms) should be used, and defer to a future paper and to Basu-DasGupta.
papers.detail: Class of procedures: a single fixed statistic, the t-test/interval (the 's-test' is t with reduced d.f.); it is optimal only in the sense of minimal critical values among tests with sup-size <= alpha within the Gaussian-mixture family, not optimal among all location-scale equivariant procedures, and there is no impossibility result over a procedure class. Class of distributions: Gaussian scale mixtures (symmetric, unimodal, smooth) only; no atoms, no finite population, no without-replacement sampling. Result is that finite valid critical values exist for every alpha and every n>=2 (critical values in Table 1 for n-1>=2 and the n=2 Cauchy case is covered by t_1), i.e. there is NO nonexistence threshold of the form n vs log2(1/alpha) in this class. The only 'impossibility' is for x<1 (|T_n|=1 exactly when n-1 of the sigma's are 0, so the t-statistic has modulus 1), a threshold independent of n and alpha. Extremality: worst case = k equal nonzero scales and n-k zero scales (n-k observations tied exactly at mu), maximised over k; this is structurally reminiscent of (A)'s 'population constant on G-k clusters' extremal, and for k=1 (one live observation) is the exact analogue of a spike population, but it is a with-replacement Gaussian-mixture statement about the t statistic, with no max-share kappa, no fpc, no sampling design, no equivariance class and no fixed-coefficient/fitted-coefficient distinction. It is not a two-point/coin-flip worst case in the sense of (A): the extremal law is a mixture of point mass at mu and Gaussians, not a two-point population. (The Rademacher-type sum in the Efron 1969 sign-symmetry representation is mentioned only through references.) Nothing on (B).

papers.paper: Basu & DasGupta (1995), Robustness of standard confidence intervals for location parameters under departure from normality, Ann. Statist. 23(4):1433-1442
papers.pages_read: All 10, as rendered page images (full text, theorems, proofs, tables, references).
papers.what_it_proves: Setting: X_i = theta + sigma Z_i, Z_i i.i.d. from F in a class; coverage of the t-interval, rho_t(F) = P_F(|T_n|<=t), and its infimum over F. F_1 = symmetric unimodal: Thm 1 (Benjamini, quoted): stretching order => coverage ordering for t>=n-1. Thm 2: for t>=n-1 inf over F_1 is attained at U[-1,1]. Cor 1: n=2, inf = t/(t+1) for t>=1. Thm 3 (n=2): inf = 0 for all t<1, via X_i = sign(U_i)|U_i|^{1/a}, a->0, coverage (1/2)[1-((1-t)/(1+t))^a]. Thm 4: for ANY family closed under scale and mixtures of continuous-at-0 symmetric laws, inf coverage = 0 for all n>=2 when t<1 (mixture with a tiny-probability huge-scale component makes one observation dominate so |T_n|~1; proof sketched, details in an unpublished tech report). Numerics: threshold t_n below n-1 (Table 1, n<=10) beyond which U[-1,1] is extremal; Table 2 of minimum coverage. Conjecture 1 (numerically checked to n=10, NOT proved): over orthant-symmetric Z, inf P(S_n^2<=s) = 1-2^{-k} for k<=s<k+1, k=1..n-1. Thm 5/6: for symmetric-contamination and arbitrary epsilon-contamination of N(0,1), the independent-embedding infimum is attained with contaminating G* a symmetric two-point law (+-v) or a two-point mean-zero law (Mulholland-Rogers extreme-point argument); numerics suggest the minimiser is i.i.d. P-value robustness discussion in Sec. 4.
papers.detail: Procedure class: only the t-interval (and z-interval remark). Population class: infinite, i.i.d., symmetric (unimodal / orthant-symmetric / contamination). No finite population, no SRSWOR, no fpc, no equivariance class beyond the scale invariance of T_n, no max-share kappa, no fixed vs fitted coefficient. The 't<1 gives coverage 0' result is the analogue of (A)'s 'kappa -> 1 spike makes the interval useless' phenomenon but is a statement about one specific statistic over all n, with a threshold t=1 that does not depend on n or alpha, not an n vs log2(1/alpha) law. TWO-POINT EXTREMALITY: Thm 5 and Thm 6 give two-point extremal CONTAMINATING distributions G* (symmetric +-v; mean-zero two-point), derived by a convex-hull/extreme-point argument for the t-statistic coverage in a contamination class around N(0,1). This is two-point in a different sense (mixture component), proved for a specific statistic and class; it does not coincide with, imply, or specialise to (A)'s two-point populations (constant on G-k clusters, extremal over all valid equivariant intervals, via kappa >= (1-k/G)/k). COIN-FLIP: Conjecture 1 is the only 2^{-k} object (1-2^{-k} for s in [k,k+1)), unproved, for orthant-symmetric vectors and sign-flip mixtures W_xi = sum xi_i Delta_i with Delta_i Rademacher; at k=n-1 it equals 1-2^{-(n-1)}, the same number as Lanke's variation-interval coverage. It concerns the statistic S_n^2 over orthant-symmetric laws, not intervals over a procedure class, and is a conjecture. Nothing on (B).

papers.paper: Gleser & Hwang (1987), The nonexistence of 100(1-alpha)% confidence sets of finite expected diameter in errors-in-variables and related models, Ann. Statist. 15(4):1351-1362
papers.pages_read: All 12, as rendered page images (read in full including proofs of Thms 1-3, applications, comments, references).
papers.what_it_proves: Setting: parametric model Y ~ f(y|theta), theta=(theta1,theta2); nuisance theta2 has a limit point theta2* where the density limit is independent of theta1 (cond. 1.5), and gamma(theta1) has unbounded range over a set Theta1*. Thm 1: every confidence set C(Y) with confidence 1-alpha>0 has P_theta(diam C = infinity) > 0 for all theta; hence infinite expected diameter, and any finite-diameter set has confidence 0. Proof: coverage <= lim over theta2->theta2* (dominated convergence), then let gamma(theta1)->infinity. Thm 2: vector extension via Scheffe projections. Thm 3: if gamma has finite range [a,b], any confidence interval with confidence >1/2 contains [a,b] with positive probability for all theta. Applications: linear/nonlinear errors-in-variables (beta1 slopes), principal-component vectors, ratios of regression coefficients and inverse regression (Fieller), mixing proportions, von Mises location. Comments: large-sample intervals fail uniformly.
papers.detail: Qualitative nonexistence over parametric families with a non-identifiability limit point; no finite populations, no sampling design, no explicit bound on the probability of an unbounded interval (only '>0'), no n vs alpha threshold, no equivariance class, no max-share kappa, no extremal two-point/spike population, no minimax-design result. The mechanism is the same type of argument (coverage of any valid set is bounded by its coverage in a degenerate limit where the target is unidentified), and its Thm 3 (confidence > 1/2 forces containing the entire range with positive probability) echoes 'unbounded w.p. >= pi(k*-1)-alpha' only in spirit, because (A) gives an explicit lower bound pi(k*-1)-alpha under EVERY population in a finite-population SRSWOR design. Nothing on (B): no least-squares-fitted coefficient, GREG/PPI++, leverage, or residual affine-in-f_S defeating samples. Relevant as a citation for the general principle 'valid confidence sets must be unbounded with positive probability when the nuisance can degenerate', not as an occurrence of either result.

lanke_threshold: Lanke's Theorem 2 states: for no alpha < 2^{-n+1} do there exist real, locally bounded (g_L,g_R) on R^n with P(g_L(X)<theta<g_R(X))>=1-alpha for all i.i.d. samples from continuous distributions symmetric about theta. That is n < 1 + log2(1/alpha) = log2(2/alpha) impossible, and it is sharp via Theorem 1 at lam=0 (the variation interval has miscoverage exactly 2^{-(n-1)}). Procedure class: ALL locally bounded measurable endpoint pairs, with no equivariance assumed (location-scale equivariance is not used; the proof is a pure translation argument with two far-apart uniform clusters). Populations: continuous symmetric laws only (uniform on [-1,1] union [2theta-1,2theta+1], which has a non-unique median; a remark says it can be perturbed to a unique median at the cost of 2^{-n} -> (2+eps)^{-n}). No atoms are treated, but impossibility over a subclass carries over to any larger class. Endpoints must be finite reals (infinite intervals excluded). CAVEAT: the printed proof explicitly derives only the one-sided bound gamma >= 2^{-n} (i.e. alpha<2^{-n}, n<log2(1/alpha)) and says it is 'obviously sufficient'; the factor of 2 needed for the stated alpha<2^{-n+1} is not shown and I could not reconstruct it. So the claimed sharp threshold is 1+log2(1/alpha) (as the theorem states), but the rigorously displayed one is log2(1/alpha).
overall_A: Not contained. No paper treats a finite population with SRSWOR, the fpc-t interval, max-share kappa, pi(k)/k*, kappa2(k*-1), the 'unbounded w.p. >= pi(k*-1)-alpha under every population' statement, two-point/constant-on-G-k extremal populations over all valid equivariant intervals, or SRS minimaxity among fixed-size designs. What does exist: (i) the large-G smallest-kappa0 NUMBER n<1+log2(1/alpha) appears as Lanke's Theorem 2 statement for an infinite i.i.d. symmetric-centre problem with arbitrary locally bounded procedures (proof printed only for 2^{-n}, factor-2 step not displayed); (ii) Basu-DasGupta Thm 3/4 and Bakirov-Szekely Thm 1 give the spike/dominant-observation phenomenon (|T_n|=1, t<1 gives zero coverage / sup tail 1) for the t statistic, which is the k=1 analogue of (A)'s spike population but with an n- and alpha-independent threshold; Bakirov-Szekely's extremal 'k live scales, n-k tied at mu' is structurally similar to 'constant on G-k clusters' but is a with-replacement Gaussian-mixture statement about one statistic; (iii) Basu-DasGupta's two-point extremal contaminations (Thm 5/6) and the unproved coin-flip Conjecture 1 (inf = 1-2^{-k}) are different objects from (A)'s two-point extremality; (iv) Gleser-Hwang gives only the qualitative 'positive probability of infinite diameter' principle. Verdict: the finite-population exact threshold (kappa-dependent critical value, pi(k) formula, extremality, design minimax) remains unclaimed by these four papers; only its infinite-population limit number is pre-empted (by Lanke, up to the factor-2 caveat).
overall_B: Not contained in any of the four papers. None involves a coefficient fitted by least squares on the sample, GREG/PPI++, leverage h_gg, residuals exactly affine in f_S as defeating samples, an f-dependent kappa_dagger, or spike max-share formulas; none treats a finite population or survey design at all. Gleser-Hwang's errors-in-variables non-identifiability argument is the nearest in spirit (degenerate-limit parameter forces unbounded intervals) but is parametric and unrelated to fitted-coefficient regression adjustment.
deviations: Bakirov-Szekely (9 pp) and Lanke (6 pp) were read from the PDF text layer, not as page images: the page images queued by read_file were not delivered to me. Lanke p.3 (Theorem 2) was additionally checked as a rendered image. Bakirov-Szekely formulas are legible in the extraction but were not cross-checked against images.

The two scans (Gleser-Hwang 12 pp, Basu-DasGupta 10 pp) were rendered locally with pypdfium2 (no OCR available) and read as images with host.view_image; the temporary renderings were deleted afterwards and nothing from the papers was saved as an artifact. Nothing in the refs folder was modified.

Basu-DasGupta's proof of Thm 4 is only sketched in the paper (details in an unpublished technical report), and its Table 1/2 numerics and Conjecture 1 are reported as the authors' numerical claims, not verified by me. I did not re-derive any theorem or run any computation.
